Scientia Visionis
sĭ-ĕn´shĭ-ă vĭ-zē-ō´nĭs
n. phrase (Latin: God's knowledge of vision; His knowledge of what He has actually decreed, as distinct from mere possibles and from Molina's middle knowledge)
Latin scientia, knowledge, + visionis, of vision. The older school named three: knowledge of simple intelligence (what is possible), knowledge of vision (what is and will be, because decreed), and, with Molina, a middle knowledge of what free creatures would do. The Reformed keep the first two and refuse the third as a God who looks before He wills.

Biblical Definition

Scientia visionis is God's knowledge of the world He has actually willed, not a catalog of unused options. Isaiah's God declares the end from the beginning: “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10). Known unto Him are all His works: “Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world” (Act 15:18). The darkness is not dark to Him: “Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day” (Psa 139:12). And the word is not a guess about what we might do. It is the word that makes: “The Lord of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass” (Isa 14:24). Hebrews puts the finished view in one clause: “Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do” (Heb 4:13). Vision here is not eyesight. It is the knowledge of what is, because He willed it.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for the Latin phrase. Scientia visionis is the scholastic name for God's knowledge of actuals, as distinct from possibles and from middle knowledge.

SCIENTIA VISIONIS, Latin, knowledge of vision. Scholastic phrase, not an 1828 English headword.

God's knowledge of what is, has been, and will be, because He has decreed it.

Distinct from scientia simplicis intelligentiae (possibles) and from Molina's scientia media.

The biblical cargo is Acts 15:18 and Isaiah 46:10: known works, declared end, standing counsel.

Key Scripture

Isa 46:10 — "Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:"

Act 15:18 — "Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world."

Psa 139:12 — "Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee."

Isa 14:24 — "The LORD of hosts hath sworn, saying, Surely as I have thought, so shall it come to pass; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand:"

Heb 4:13 — "Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do."

Modern Corruption

Vision-knowledge is either reduced to a forecast of our freedom, or inflated into a stare that never decides, and Isaiah's God declares because He will do.

expand to see more

Molina's middle knowledge sits between possibles and actuals and claims to know what the creature would do if placed. The dictionary already answered that on the middle-knowledge page. Scientia visionis is the older name for the knowledge that does not wait on that would. Isaiah 46:10 joins declaring and doing in one breath. The end is declared because the pleasure will be done.

Open theism hears vision and thinks God is watching a game He did not script. Acts 15:18 is not sports commentary. Known unto God are all His works from the beginning of the world. The works are His. The knowing is not a later report.

Hebrews 4:13 is why the phrase still matters in a pulpit. All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with whom we have to do. That is not a threat that God might be surprised by a better story. It is the comfort that nothing in the story is off His book, and the warning that nothing in the story is off His book.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin scientia visionis; Hebrew nagad (H5046), to declare; Greek gnostos (G1110), known.

Latin scientia visionis — knowledge of actuals; not middle knowledge.

Hebrew nagad (H5046) — to declare; Isaiah 46:10, declaring the end from the beginning.

Greek gnostos (G1110) — known; Acts 15:18, known unto God are all his works.

Usage

"“Declaring the end from the beginning” — vision, not a forecast."

"“Known unto God are all his works” — His works, from the beginning."

"“Naked and opened unto the eyes” — with whom we have to do."
